_about: Evidence-backed policy recommendation cards. Each follows the CLAUDE.md recommendation rules (problem, location, evidence, mechanism, intervention, equity check, confidence, uncertainty) and links to proven countermeasures (data/countermeasures.json) plus a filtered map view. These are analyst-drafted starting points for human review, NOT automated or final policy.

recommendations.title: Prioritize a low-cost pedestrian-safety package east of the river
recommendations.problem: Severe crashes concentrate in a few wards and fall hardest on people walking. Wards 7 and 8 carry an outsized share of killed-or-seriously-injured cases relative to their population.

evidence.claim: The three highest-burden wards account for ~49% of citywide KSI since 2024.

Those same three wards (2, 7, and 8) are home to only ~36% of residents (ward population estimates on current boundaries; 2020 U.S. Census total 689,545), underscoring a KSI burden out of proportion to population.
evidence.source_title: Ward population estimates — DC Office of Planning / DC Health Matters; 2020 U.S. Census total

evidence.claim: Pedestrians made up ~235 KSI in 2024-present with a high share of deaths, second only to drivers citywide.

recommendations.mechanism: Layering daylighting, curb extensions, leading pedestrian intervals, and lower speeds onto routine repaving improves sight lines, shortens crossings, and cuts impact speeds where pedestrians are most exposed.
recommendations.equity_check: Wards 7 and 8 have faced historic transportation disinvestment; investing engineering here addresses a disparate burden. The package is engineering-led, avoiding enforcement-heavy approaches that can fall unevenly.
recommendations.uncertainty: Ward grain is coarse; exact corridors need an intersection/HIN-level join. Recent-year counts are preliminary. KSI shares use a fixed population denominator.

recommendations.title: Target speed management on the High Injury Network
recommendations.problem: Speed-involved crashes raise injury severity, and a small set of corridors carries most severe crashes. Enforcement alone is uneven; it should accompany engineering.

evidence.claim: Speeding is flagged in thousands of DC crashes and concentrates on higher-speed arterials.
A DDOT study reported ~20% fewer injuries around enforced locations (841 to 673 injury crashes).

recommendations.mechanism: Road diets and lower limits reduce top-end speeds by design; automated enforcement reinforces them where geometry can't be changed quickly, lowering the speeds that drive crash severity.
recommendations.equity_check: Automated enforcement can burden some communities disproportionately; lead with engineering, site cameras transparently on the HIN, and monitor ticket distribution.
recommendations.uncertainty: Per-corridor HIN crash counts are now computed (data/hin-corridors.json); the citywide share of KSI carried by the HIN is not yet computed. Before/after camera effects are subject to regression-to-the-mean.

recommendations.title: Scale cheap, systemic fixes to reverse the rising-deaths trend
recommendations.problem: DC set a goal of zero deaths and serious injuries by 2024 and did not meet it; traffic deaths rose through the early 2020s, peaking around 50 in 2024.

evidence.claim: DC averaged ~43 traffic deaths a year in 2020-2024, peaking at 50 in 2024 — the target year.
evidence.source_title: Computed from Crashes in DC by year

evidence.claim: Hoboken NJ reached multiple consecutive years with zero traffic deaths using low-cost measures on routine repaving.

recommendations.mechanism: Systematically applying proven low-cost countermeasures across the network during repaving cycles compounds small safety gains citywide rather than waiting on large capital projects.
recommendations.equity_check: A systemic program should sequence by injury burden so historically disinvested wards are not last; keep the prioritization components visible.
recommendations.uncertainty: Open-data counts may differ from DDOT's curated figures; 2025-2026 are preliminary. Causal attribution of any future decline requires before/after evaluation.

recommendations.title: Close the DC crossing-guard gap and expand school-zone safety programs
recommendations.problem: DDOT staffs 214 crossing-guard posts across 135 schools for the 2025-2026 school year, but coverage is not published by ward, and many school crossings near high-crash corridors in Wards 7 and 8 — where student density and pedestrian crash risk are high — may lack a guarded crossing.
recommendations.location_scope: All DC schools, prioritized by student enrollment and nearby crash history

evidence.claim: School-zone safety packages combine trained crossing guards with engineering (high-visibility crosswalks, curb extensions, leading pedestrian intervals) and 20 mph limits; lower impact speeds sharply raise a struck child's odds of survival.

DDOT commits crossing-guard coverage to 214 posts over 135 schools across the District for the 2025-2026 school year; per-ward coverage shares are not published, so the size of any gap in Wards 7 and 8 is not officially quantified.

recommendations.mechanism: Combine trained crossing guards at high-volume school crossings with engineering (daylighting, bump-outs, LPI) and low speed limits to create safe passage for children.
recommendations.equity_check: Prioritize schools in Wards 7 and 8 for first-phase crossing-guard funding. Combine with pedestrian-safety education for students.
recommendations.uncertainty: DDOT does not publish crossing-guard coverage by ward, so the size of any Ward 7/8 gap is unquantified; the case rests on documented school-zone-safety benefits rather than a measured local coverage shortfall. Causal effect of crossing guards alone vs. combined with infrastructure is not disaggregated in local data. Implementation cost assumes $40–$60K per school for full coverage.

recommendations.title: Deploy protected intersections on the top high-injury corridors
recommendations.problem: Georgia Ave NW, Alabama Ave SE, Connecticut Ave NW, New York Ave NE, and 14th St NW carry the most people killed or seriously injured among DDOT High Injury Network corridors. Standard intersections allow turning vehicles to conflict with pedestrians and cyclists.
recommendations.location_scope: Top HIN corridors by KSI: Georgia Ave NW, Alabama Ave SE, Connecticut Ave NW, New York Ave NE, 14th St NW (see the Hotspots page for the full ranking and per-corridor counts)

evidence.claim: Protected intersections (corner islands, setback crossings, dedicated signal phases) reduce fatal/major-injury crashes by 50–70% at peer-city sites (NYC, Seattle, Vancouver).

These corridors are the highest-KSI segments of the DDOT High Injury Network, computed by joining Open Data DC crash records to the HIN (crashes within 25 m of the centerline, 2022-present); per-corridor counts and a record-level audit trail are in data/hin-corridors.json.
evidence.source_title: DC Vision Zero high-injury corridors (crashes × HIN spatial join)

recommendations.mechanism: Redesign conflict points so pedestrians cross in a protected phase with no turning traffic, or cross in refuge islands with reduced conflict exposure. Pair with LPI and speed enforcement.
recommendations.equity_check: Alabama Ave SE serves Wards 7 and 8 and Georgia Ave NW spans Wards 1 and 4 (equity priorities). Community engagement required on each corridor.
recommendations.uncertainty: Per-corridor counts are now data-derived, but cost per intersection ($500K–$1.5M) and timeline (6–9 months design + build) need budget and phasing clarity, and a before/after evaluation framework is still needed.

recommendations.title: Install adaptive traffic signal control with pedestrian detection on major intersections
recommendations.problem: Fixed signal timing does not adapt to real-time demand, creating dilemma zones where drivers rear-end each other and pedestrians get stuck in the roadway. Pedestrian detection is missing at many high-volume crossings.
recommendations.location_scope: Major corridors: New York Ave NE, H Street NW/NE, South Capitol Street, Georgia Avenue NW (10–15 intersections)

evidence.claim: Adaptive signal control + pedestrian detection reduces crashes at busy intersections by 15–25% (research-grade; verify locally before widespread deployment).

recommendations.mechanism: Real-time signal timing adjusts to vehicle and pedestrian demand, reducing rear-end crashes and pedestrian-vehicle conflicts at bottleneck intersections.
recommendations.equity_check: Prioritize high-volume corridors serving lower-income wards (Wards 7, 8 connections).
recommendations.uncertainty: Cost ($150K–$500K per intersection) and maintenance burden must be modeled. Local before/after study needed to confirm effect size.
